claims.text: A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested by collecting data, analysing it and drawing a conclusion from the evidence; an aim says what the enquiry sets out to find, and the hypothesis is the claim about the answer that the data will confirm or reject.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A testable hypothesis names the places, the measure and the expected direction: that the bedload of the river becomes smaller and rounder downstream, or that pedestrian counts fall with distance from the CBD, so the data has something definite to confirm or reject.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A questionnaire succeeds by its layout, the format and wording of its questions and their number: a clear uncluttered layout, a mix of closed questions that are quick to tally and one or two open ones, wording that is short, neutral and free of jargon, and few enough questions that a stranger answers in two or three minutes.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Question wording decides the answer's worth: leading questions that suggest the answer, double questions that ask two things at once and technical terms the respondent may not know each damage the data, so each question asks one plain thing.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A pilot survey is a small trial of the questionnaire that tests its questions and method on a few people first, so that unclear wording, missing answer boxes and overlong interviews are fixed before the real survey wastes its day.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Random sampling gives every person or point an equal chance of being chosen, systematic sampling takes every nth person or point at regular intervals, and stratified sampling samples groups in proportion to their share of the whole; the choice of method decides whether the sample represents the population.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A survey method is justified by what it measures, not by convenience: the reason names what the method captures and what would go wrong without it, rather than calling it easy or cheap.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Observation records what is seen on the spot: positions marked on a base map, counts and notes on a recording sheet, a field sketch drawn from one fixed viewpoint with a frame and scale, and annotated photographs that label the features the enquiry needs.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A recording sheet for a count carries its identifying details, time, date, location and the recorder's name, so that two sheets can be compared fairly; counts at different sites are made at the same time of day so the time of day is not the variable that explains the difference.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A count has two designs: a tally count of everything passing in a set period, or a timing count of how long a set number takes, and the choice is made by how many are expected, because a busy site needs a timing count and a quiet site needs a tally.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Physical measurement uses its own instruments: a quadrat frames a known area for vegetation counts, a clinometer measures slope angle between two ranging poles, and callipers or a pebbleometer measures stone size, each sited and sampled so the measurements are reliable.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: River measurements are made in a marked channel cross-section: width bank to bank with a tape, depth at equal intervals with a metre rule, speed by timing a float over a measured 10-metre distance between ranging poles, and bedload size and shape from a sample of stones.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A beach profile is measured with a clinometer between ranging poles set at the top and bottom of each facet of the slope, pebble size and shape are sampled at fixed points along a transect, and the movement of beach material can be traced with marked pebbles.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Weather instruments are sited so they measure the air, not their surroundings: a rain gauge sunk into open level ground away from trees and buildings, a Stevenson screen for the thermometers on short grass away from walls, an anemometer and wind vane in the open, all read at the same time each day.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A rain gauge wrongly sited, under trees, against a wall or raised on a table, collects too little rain or splashed extra, and parts that are not known cannot be read, so the siting rules are part of the measurement.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Human fieldwork counts and surveys have standard designs: pedestrian and traffic counts at set points for set minutes, land-use surveys on a base map with a category key, and environmental quality surveys scored site by site on a fixed scale.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Each graph type suits its data: lines for time series, bars for categories, divided bars and pies for shares, flow diagrams for movement, wind-roses for wind frequency by direction, isoline maps for values over space, scatter graphs with best-fit lines for relationships, and kite diagrams for changing proportions along a line.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Completing a graph follows the conventions of the page: the same scale as the printed part, the key's shading and order, pie segments clockwise from the top, and bars rising from the correct end of the axis.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Describing results states the overall pattern first, the direction and size of change, then the exception, and supports each with figures read from the table or graph, with units and the sites or dates they came from.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A conclusion states whether the hypothesis is true, false or partly true, and then supports the decision with paired figures from the data, the sites and their values, because a decision without figures is an opinion.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A hypothesis judged without evidence from the data is not a conclusion: the decision needs a figure that proves it, the values at two sites or two dates that show the pattern the hypothesis claimed or denied.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Reliability means the method would give the same results if repeated, and an evaluation names what to change and why the change makes the results more reliable, more sites, a larger sample, a different time or season, or a method less open to error.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Repeating the enquiry unchanged is not an improvement by itself: the improvement names what is done differently and what defect it fixes, otherwise the same errors return with the same results.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An extension tests something new, another place, another season or another variable, so the new enquiry answers a different question rather than repeating the original.

claims.text: A questionnaire's questions are built one per fact the hypothesis needs, closed and banded for tallying, with a single open question for reasons, and the whole form answerable in two or three minutes.

claims.text: A survey session runs to plan at a fixed location, sampled by a stated rule, piloted first so the wording faults are caught while they are cheap to fix, and every sheet carries its identifying details.

claims.text: An observation survey records each feature twice, on the base map for pattern and on the recording sheet for detail, with a photograph numbered where a judgement is close, so the record can be checked later by someone who was not there.

claims.text: A school weather station sited by the rules, gauges in the open away from obstacles, screen over mown grass, wind instruments clear of parapets, all read at the same time daily and reset after reading, produces a series the study can use.
